did_you_know.text: Did you know? In this chapter, the word "shepherds" is a metaphor for Israel’s leaders: they are expected to care for the flock, but are portrayed as caring for themselves instead of the people.

Did you know? Ezekiel lists six responsibilities of a responsible leader: strengthening the weak, healing the sick, bandaging the injured, bringing back the straying, searching for the lost, and tending the flock gently.
Did you know? After criticizing the shepherds, the Lord declares that he himself will search for his flock and care for it—a major shift from failed human leadership to direct divine care.

Did you know? The gathering of the flock is described as bringing it out from among the nations and lands and returning it to the land of Israel. Thus, the image of shepherding also includes gathering the exiles.

Did you know? The Lord promises not only to gather the flock but also to care for its different needs: he will search for the lost, bring back the straying, bandage the injured, and strengthen the sick; but he will judge the strong who oppress the others.

Did you know? The judgment in this chapter is directed not only at the shepherds but also at the flock itself: the Lord judges between one sheep and another and between the strong and the weak within the community.
Did you know? Alongside the promise that the Lord will shepherd his flock, he says that he will appoint over them "one shepherd"—David his servant—who will lead Israel.
Did you know? The vision of restoration includes a "covenant of peace" and protection from wild animals; in this chapter, peace also means practical protection for the people’s lives.
Did you know? The blessing is also expressed through nature: rain will fall at the proper time, and it is called "showers of blessing."

Did you know? The chapter ends by clarifying that the flock is not merely a metaphor for animals: "you are my sheep" refers to human beings, especially the house of Israel, whom the Lord identifies as his people.
